intro: Every week in Chicago, in cathedrals and storefront churches, in Spanish, Polish, Korean and English, Christians read aloud from the New Testament. It is a small collection, twenty-seven writings in all, composed in Greek within about a century. Yet it shapes the worship of more than two billion Christians and much of the world's art, law and language. In this unit you will study it the way scholars do: as texts with authors, audiences and purposes.

Chapter 5 opens the four Gospels. You will meet first-century Judea under Rome, compare how Matthew, Mark, Luke and John tell the life of Jesus, and read the Sermon on the Mount and the parables. Chapter 6 follows the movement outward through Acts and Paul's letters and into the visions of Revelation. It ends with how the churches chose their canon, wrote their creeds and divided into Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant branches.

Along the way you will practice the method from unit 1. Attribute every belief: Christians believe, Paul teaches, historians argue. Notice where Jewish and Christian readings of the same passage differ. By the end you should be able to read a Gospel passage or a letter closely, explain what it meant to its first audience, and describe how different Christians read it today.
bigQuestion: How did the writings of a small first-century Jewish movement become the New Testament, and how do different readers understand them today?

timeline.t: The Roman general Pompey brings Judea under Roman power
Jesus is crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate (estimates range from about 30 to 33)
Paul's experience on the road to Damascus, by common estimates
The Council of Jerusalem decides Gentile believers need not be circumcised
Paul writes First Thessalonians, probably the oldest surviving Christian writing
Paul writes First Corinthians from Ephesus
Rome destroys the Jerusalem Temple; many scholars date Mark to about this time
Matthew, Luke, Acts and John are written, by common scholarly estimates
The Council of Nicaea produces the first form of the Nicene Creed
Athanasius lists the twenty-seven books of the New Testament
Leaders in Rome and Constantinople excommunicate each other
Martin Luther's ninety-five theses begin the Protestant Reformation

words.d: from an Old English word for good news; one of the four accounts of the life of Jesus: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
seen together; the name for Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share much material
a short story from ordinary life that carries a deeper meaning and asks the hearer to respond
in the Gospels, God's rule over the world, which Christians believe began with Jesus and is still to come
from a Latin word for suffering; the last week of Jesus' life, from his entry into Jerusalem to his death
rising from the dead; Christians believe God raised Jesus on the third day
one who is sent; Jesus' closest followers and leaders such as Paul who spread the message
in Christian teaching, God's free gift of love and favor, which cannot be earned
a letter; the older English name for the letters of the New Testament
the official list of books a community accepts as scripture
from the Latin credo, I believe; a short summary of faith said together, such as the Nicene Creed

test.q: Who governed Judea as the Roman prefect when Jesus was crucified?
test.why: Pilate governed Judea from about 26 to 36 CE, and the Gospels place the trial before him.

test.q: Which Gospel do most scholars think was written first?
test.why: Most scholars date Mark to about 70 CE and think Matthew and Luke used it as a source.

choices: A short story from ordinary life that carries a deeper meaning and asks the hearer to respond
A vision of the end of the world
test.why: Parables such as the Good Samaritan use everyday scenes and leave the hearer to answer.

test.q: Which Gospel opens with the words In the beginning was the Word?
test.why: John 1:1 echoes Genesis and calls Jesus the Word, or Logos.

test.q: In the Good Samaritan, why was the Samaritan a surprising hero for Luke's first hearers?
choices: Jews and Samaritans were hostile to each other
He was one of the twelve disciples
test.why: Jews and Samaritans avoided each other, so the hero came from the group hearers least expected.

test.q: What does the phrase kingdom of God mean in the Synoptic Gospels?
choices: God's rule, already arriving and still to come
test.why: The kingdom of God means God's reign, which the Gospels present as begun but not finished.

test.q: Which book tells how the followers of Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome?
test.why: Acts, by the author of Luke, follows the movement from Pentecost in Jerusalem to Paul in Rome.

test.q: What did the Council of Jerusalem decide around 49 CE?
choices: That Paul should go to Rome
That the Temple should be rebuilt
That Revelation belonged in the canon
That Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised
test.why: Acts 15 says the apostles and elders decided Gentile believers need not be circumcised.

test.q: Which letter is Paul's longest and fullest statement on faith and grace?
test.why: Romans, written about 57 CE, lays out Paul's argument on justification by faith at length.

test.q: How does the Letter of James figure in debates over Paul's teaching on faith?
choices: It says faith alone saves without any works
It says faith without works is dead, a line Catholics and Protestants interpret differently
It rejects the idea of faith
test.why: Catholic and Orthodox teaching cites James on faith and works; Protestants read it as faith shown in action.

test.q: Which of these sources is the earliest written statement that Jesus was raised and appeared to his followers?
choices: Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians
test.why: First Corinthians 15, written about 55 CE, predates every Gospel.

test.q: What kind of writing uses visions, beasts and symbolic numbers to reveal hidden meaning in history?
test.why: Revelation and Daniel are apocalyptic writings, from the Greek for unveiling.

test.q: What did Athanasius do in 367 CE?
choices: He listed the twenty-seven books of today's New Testament
He wrote the Gospel of Mark
He called the Council of Nicaea
test.why: His Easter letter of 367 is the earliest known list matching the New Testament exactly.

test.q: How do Christian and Jewish readings of Isaiah 53 often differ?
choices: Both read the servant as Paul
Christians often read the servant as Jesus; many Jewish readers read the servant as Israel
Jews read the servant as Jesus and Christians read it as Israel
Neither tradition reads Isaiah 53 at all
test.why: Christians read Isaiah through the New Testament; Jewish commentators such as Rashi read the servant as Israel.

test.q: Which branch of Christianity grew out of the Reformation of the 1500s?
test.why: Luther's protest of 1517 grew into the Reformation and the Protestant churches.

write.prompt: Is love of neighbor the center of the New Testament? Cite two or three texts from this unit, such as Luke 10, Matthew 5 and First Corinthians 13. Explain what each says, what it meant to its first audience, and how different Christians have read it.
tips: Name each text with its book, chapter and verse.
Attribute every belief: Jesus teaches in Luke, Paul writes, Christians believe.
Explain the first audience, such as a law scholar in Luke 10 or the quarreling church in Corinth.
Compare readings, such as Catholic and Protestant, without judging which one is right.
Use the unit's terms, such as parable, agape and kingdom of God.
